God
GOD
n. (the proper name and title of the one living and true God; in the Authorized Version rendering Hebrew 'el, 'eloah, 'elōhīm and Greek theos)
From Old English god, common Germanic (Gothic guþ, Old High German got), of uncertain ultimate root — probably from Proto-Germanic *gudan, a neuter noun meaning “that which is invoked” or “that which is poured to” in libation. The Anglo-Saxon evangelists took a heathen word and put it under the discipline of Scripture, capitalizing it and confining it to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In the Authorized Version God renders the Hebrew 'elōhīm (a plural of majesty governing singular verbs) and the Greek theos; LORD in small capitals renders the covenant name YHWH, which is a distinct thing and must not be confused with it.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

God is the one living and true God, eternal, infinite, most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions, immutable, immense, almighty, every way infinite, most holy, most wise, most free, most absolute, working all things according to the counsel of His own immutable and most righteous will, for His own glory. Scripture never argues for His existence; it opens by assuming it — “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Gen 1:1). He names Himself to Moses as sheer self-existent being, “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14), the ground of the doctrine of aseity: He has life in Himself and derives nothing from anything outside Himself. He is one in essence — “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4) — and three in Person: Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, the same in substance, equal in power and glory. He is spirit, and therefore worshipped in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24), never through image or likeness. The word occurs 4,367 times in the Authorized Version, more than any other substantive in Scripture; it is the subject of the first sentence of the Bible and the last blessing of Revelation. Everything else in this dictionary is defined in relation to Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

The one living and true God: eternal, self-existent, simple, immutable, almighty, most holy, one in essence and three in Person — Father, Son, and Holy Ghost — the Creator, Preserver, and Governor of all things, and the chief end of man.

expand to see more

GOD, n. 1. The Supreme Being; Jehovah; the eternal and infinite spirit, the creator, and the sovereign of the universe. God is a spirit; and they that worship him, must worship him in spirit and in truth. John 4.

2. A false god; a heathen deity; an idol. Fear not the gods of the Amorites. Judges 6. Webster's 1828 entry preserves the distinction the Authorized Version keeps throughout: the word is used absolutely of the true God and derivatively of the idols the nations set in His place.

3. A person or thing exalted to the place of supreme regard; whatever a man makes his ultimate trust. “Whose god is their belly” (Php 3:19). This third sense is not a metaphor loosely used but the biblical definition of idolatry.

The confessional definition stands behind every use of the word in this dictionary. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689) 2.1 reads: “The Lord our God is but one only living and true God; whose subsistence is in and of himself, infinite in being and perfection, whose essence cannot be comprehended by any but himself; a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions, who only hath immortality.”

The name is not a genus into which the God of Scripture is placed as one instance. When the Bible says God, it does not mean a member of the class of deities distinguished by superior attributes; it means the only one there is, beside whom there is no other (Isa 45:5), and every other claimant is by definition an idol.

Key Scripture

Gen 1:1 — "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth."

Exo 3:14 — "And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you."

Deu 6:4 — "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:"

Joh 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

Modern Corruption

The modern corruption of the word God is not chiefly atheism but domestication: a warm, agreeable, permissive deity assembled from therapeutic sentiment, who affirms whatever the worshipper already wanted — and, on the academic side, the Open Theist and process denial of the very attributes the word has always carried.

expand to see more

The reigning American deity has been named accurately by sociologists as Moralistic Therapeutic Deism: a God who wants people to be nice, who wants them to feel good about themselves, who does not need to be particularly involved except when a problem arises, and who takes good people to heaven when they die. Every clause of that is a denial of the God of Scripture — His holiness, His wrath, His providence, His justification of the ungodly by grace alone. The corruption works by subtraction: nothing is formally denied, but sovereignty, holiness, and judgment quietly cease to be mentioned, until the word God retains only the residue that flatters. A congregation can sing about this deity for years without ever once being confronted by the God who says “I AM THAT I AM.”

The academic corruption is bolder. Open Theism (Clark Pinnock, Gregory Boyd, John Sanders) denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge, making God a learner within time; process theology (following Whitehead and Hartshorne) denies immutability and omnipotence outright, reducing God to the most influential participant in a universe He does not govern. Both are departures not merely from Reformed confession but from every historic Christian creed. The Reformed answer is the classical one: God is pure act, without composition, without becoming, without succession of states — and therefore His promises cannot fail, since nothing in Him can change and nothing outside Him can compel Him. A God who might learn something tomorrow is a God whose covenant is a wager.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'elōhīm (plural of majesty, singular verbs), 'el (the Mighty), 'elyōn (Most High), and shadday (Almighty), rendered by Greek theos in the Septuagint and the New Testament; distinguished throughout the Authorized Version from the covenant name YHWH, printed LORD.

expand to see more

'elōhīm (Hebrew, Strong's H430) — the ordinary Old Testament word for God, morphologically plural but taking singular verbs when it denotes the true God; the grammar is a plural of majesty and fullness, and it stands ready for the fuller Trinitarian revelation of the New Testament without itself proving it.

'el (Hebrew, H410) — the older Semitic root, “mighty, strong”; survives in the great compound names El Shaddai, El Elyon, El Roi, and embedded in Israel, Bethel, Elijah, Daniel.

YHWH (Hebrew, H3068) — the covenant name given at the bush, rendered LORD in small capitals by the Authorized Version following the Septuagint's kyrios. It is a name, not a title, and Exo 3:14 ties it to the verb hayah, to be.

theos (Greek, G2316) — the Septuagint and New Testament rendering of both 'elōhīm and, joined to kyrios, of the covenant name; applied without qualification to the Son (Joh 1:1; Joh 20:28; Tit 2:13; Heb 1:8) and to the Spirit by implication (Act 5:3–4).

1689 London Baptist Confession, chapters 2–3 — the dictionary's confessional standard on the divine essence, the decree, and the Trinity; chapter 2.3 is the Baptist restatement of Nicene orthodoxy, including eternal generation and eternal procession.

Usage

"The Authorized Version's typography is doing doctrinal work that modern readers routinely miss: God renders 'elōhīm, Lord renders 'adōnay, and LORD in small capitals renders the covenant name. “The LORD our God is one LORD” is not repetition; it is the name and the title set side by side."

"That the corpus of this dictionary carried entries for attributes-of-god and city-of-god before it carried one for god is a parable of how theological vocabularies grow — outward from the technical terms, and only late back to the plain words the text actually uses most."

"When a man says he does not believe in God, the first pastoral question is which god he means, because the deity most often rejected in modern conversation — capricious, petty, hostile to joy — is one Scripture rejects too."
